# The Space Between Thoughts

I'm sitting in a coffee shop where the espresso machine hisses like a living thing, and I'm thinking about how we're all just passing through each other's lives, leaving barely a trace. The woman across from me is reading a book with a cracked spine—the kind that's been loved, turned over in hands a thousand times. I wonder what story has captured her so completely that she hasn't touched her latte in ten minutes.

There's something about this prompt that feels honest. Write whatever comes to you. No assignment, no thesis statement lurking at the beginning like a snake in grass. Just thoughts tumbling out like laundry from an overturned basket.

What comes to me is usually messy.

I've been thinking lately about how we curate ourselves. We edit our Instagram posts, choose the angles that make us look most like the person we want to be, delete the photos where we look tired or sad or just human. Even now, writing this, there's a part of me calculating whether these words will land right, whether they'll be interesting enough, vulnerable enough but not too vulnerable. It's exhausting, this constant performance.

But maybe that's just being alive in the twenty-first century. Maybe in 1952, someone sat in a different coffee shop—one with real china cups and no WiFi—and worried about what their neighbor thought of their lawn.

I read something yesterday about how plants communicate through fungal networks underground, sending nutrients to the plants that need them most. It's called the "wood wide web," which made me smile. There's something beautiful about that—an entire universe of connection happening beneath our feet, invisible and intricate, holding the whole system together. We think we're so isolated, but maybe we're all connected like that too, just in ways we can't see. Maybe every conversation changes the chemistry of the people involved. Maybe every kind word travels further than we know.

My friend canceled plans last week and didn't give a reason. I felt the sting of it first, that small rejection. Then I realized I was doing the same thing—canceling, avoiding, wrapped up in my own chaos like a cocoon. We're all struggling with things we don't talk about. We're all waking up at three in the morning with anxiety about things we can't control. We're all wondering if we're doing this right, whatever "this" is. And we're all too scared to admit it.

The coffee shop has gotten noisier. A group of teenagers just arrived, all movement and noise and that particular kind of carefreeness that comes before you really understand how hard things can be. I miss that sometimes—not innocence exactly, but the ability to be wholly present in a moment without narrating it to an imagined audience.

What else comes to me? That I'm afraid of wasting time. That I want to write something that matters. That I don't know what matters anymore. The news cycle is a hamster wheel of crisis, and I've stopped running. I just watch it spin. That can't be healthy, but sometimes healthy feels like a luxury.

I think about my grandmother's hands—how they were always doing something. She gardened, she cooked, she mended clothes. Never sat still. She once told me that idle hands made for a restless mind, but I think the opposite might be true. I think a restless mind is the modern condition, and we're all just trying to find ways to quiet it.

The couple sitting near the window just held hands across the table, and it was so simple and so profound that I had to look away. That's what we all want, isn't it? To be known. To be chosen. To have someone sit across from us and choose to stay.

Here's something that comes to me: I don't have this figured out. I'm in my thirties and I thought I would have answers by now. Turns out I just have better questions. The fundamental confusion hasn't changed; I've just gotten more comfortable with it. That feels like growth, maybe.

I've been thinking about letters. Real letters, written by hand and sent through the mail. My grandmother saved every card anyone ever gave her. I found them after she died—stacks of paper documenting love in handwriting. We've traded that for emails, texts, likes. Faster, but something got lost. The permanence of something physical. The knowledge that someone sat down and thought of you specifically. That takes time. That takes intention.

The espresso machine hisses again. Someone nearby is having a conversation in a language I don't understand, but the tone is clear—it's someone trying to explain something to someone else. That's what most conversations are, really. Translation attempts. We're always trying to make ourselves understood, and it so rarely works. But we keep trying anyway.

That feels important somehow.

What comes to me is gratitude for small things. This coffee. This seat. The ability to notice the woman with the loved book. The knowledge that somewhere, people are right now deciding to try again—in relationships, in work, in their faith in humanity. Somewhere, someone is laughing hard enough to snort, and they don't care who hears. Somewhere, a parent is reading to a child, creating memories neither of them will quite remember the same way.

The contradictions are real too. I want to matter but I want to disappear. I want connection but I crave solitude. I want to change but I'm afraid of transformation. I want certainty but I suspect certainty is a lie we tell ourselves to sleep better.

So here's what comes to me in the end: life is mostly about showing up. Getting in the coffee shop. Writing the words. Having the conversation even when you're not sure what to say. Being the person who notices the other person. Staying when it would be easier to leave. Trying when you're terrified of failing.

It's not revolutionary. It's just human.

And maybe that's enough.
